speaker: Matt Risinger
title: Building Science with Matt Risinger ECP 66
question: In custom home building, why do speculative builds carry asymmetric financial danger during sudden housing downturns?
guest: I totally changed my business after that last recession. I don't do any speculative builds, and any builder that comes to me and talks about it, I tell them my story and say, "I'd be really cautious about that." Because as great as a spec house is to sell today, all it takes is a month or two to change the whims of America. And all of a sudden, that speculative build that you built, you can't sell, and you're on the hook for a personal guarantee pretty much no matter what. So there's not a better time to plan for a recession or for changes in your business than today. Being really cautious about buying things on debt or doing jobs that are speculative and unsold is a great way to prepare for that next change. That's really what I've done: my business doesn't have any debt, and I don't have any personal debt.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Speculative builds are dangerous in a sudden downturn because the builder carries all of the risk with no committed buyer, while the upside is capped and the downside is not.

In a contract (pre-sold) custom build, the client owns or finances the land, funds construction through draws, and is contractually bound to a price. The builder's exposure is mostly limited to their margin. In a spec build, the builder fronts the land, materials, and labor, usually with a short-term, high-interest construction loan that is often personally guaranteed.

If the market holds, the builder earns a normal margin, perhaps 10–20 percent. If it turns, several things compound at once. The price drops, often by more than the entire margin. The home sits unsold while interest, taxes, insurance, and maintenance accumulate monthly. Costs are already sunk, and an unfinished house is worth far less than the money put into it. Lenders may also freeze draws, demand paydowns, or refuse to extend maturing loans, forcing a sale at the worst time.

Because of leverage, a modest price decline can wipe out the builder's equity entirely, and several simultaneous specs can bankrupt an otherwise healthy firm.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Unlike pre-sold custom homes, where a committed buyer locks in a contract price and funds construction draws, speculative builds require the builder to carry all land, material, and labor costs upfront using equity and short-term, often personally guaranteed construction debt. Because custom-caliber homes take a year or more to complete, builders frequently lock in peak-market input costs long before the property can be listed. This timing gap creates severe financial asymmetry: in strong markets, upside is capped by neighborhood comparables and appraisal limits, whereas in a sudden downturn, high leverage and illiquidity magnify downside losses dramatically. High-end buyer pools are thin, bespoke architectural finishes narrow appeal compared to standard tract homes, and demand freezes quickly when credit tightens—yet a mid-construction home cannot be paused without risking physical deterioration or violating loan covenants. Consequently, even a modest drop in sale price can erase the builder’s entire profit margin and equity cushion, while relentless carrying costs—floating-rate interest, taxes, insurance, and approaching loan maturities—bleed cash reserves and force steep discounts, distressed sales, or insolvency.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Speculative builds carry lopsided risk because the builder pays for everything before there's any buyer. With a contracted custom home, the client has usually paid a deposit, made progress payments and committed to the purchase. With a spec home, the builder has already sunk money into the land, permits, materials and labor, often using short-term construction loans with floating rates and personal guarantees.

When the market turns suddenly, the costs keep running while income disappears. Interest, taxes, insurance and upkeep pile up every month the house sits unsold. Buyers vanish or demand big discounts, and appraisals fall, so the house can end up worth less than what's owed on it. Lenders may cut credit lines, require more cash or refuse to extend loans when they come due.

The upside in a good market is limited to a normal builder's margin, often 10–20%. The downside can wipe out the builder's equity and more, especially when they're carrying several spec homes at once. Those projects take 6 to 18 months to finish, so they can't be stopped quickly when conditions change.

models.answer: Speculative custom builds carry asymmetric financial danger because a builder’s upside in a strong market is capped by local appraisals and comparable sales, whereas the downside in a sudden downturn is magnified by leverage, sunk peak-cycle costs, and illiquidity. Unlike pre-sold custom homes funded by a committed buyer, a spec builder finances land, materials, and labor upfront, typically through short-term, high-interest construction loans backed by personal guarantees. When housing demand abruptly stalls, those construction costs remain locked in at pre-downturn prices while the finished home’s market value falls. Simultaneously, extended days on market pile on carrying costs—interest, taxes, insurance, and maintenance—that steadily erode equity. Because custom spec homes target a narrow, discretionary buyer pool, they are especially hard to move when credit tightens. As short-term loan maturities approach, lenders may decline extensions or demand principal paydowns, forcing builders to slash prices well below total cost to avoid default. One stalled project can therefore wipe out years of accumulated profits or trigger insolvency.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A speculative builder buys the lot and finances construction before securing a buyer. Most costs are committed by the time the home goes on the market, but the sale price and timing are still uncertain. In a sudden downturn, buyers can disappear and prices can fall just as the builder needs to sell. Every extra month adds interest, taxes, insurance, and maintenance, while a construction loan may come due before a buyer shows up.

The risk is asymmetric because the expected profit is usually a small share of the sale price. If a home is expected to sell for $1 million and costs $900,000 to build and carry, a 10% price drop wipes out the entire $100,000 profit before any extra holding costs. A deeper drop can eat through the builder’s equity and leave them owing money even after the sale. A custom build with a signed buyer and progress payments typically gives the builder more predictable cash flow and less exposure to resale prices.
